newsitem.title: JAPAN: Operators ready to sell dollars on economic fears.
newsitem.headline: Operators ready to sell dollars on economic fears.

text.p: A variety of operators in Japan and overseas are standing by to sell the dollar against the yen on rallies as uncertainty over U.S. interest rates and European monetary union grows, dealers said on Friday.
A weak Japanese economic recovery and low interest rates may give operators little reason to buy the yen, but unsettling external factors have also put pressure on the dollar.
"If you look at only domestic factors, it is not a situation to buy the yen," said Kazunori Iida, a manager at Nissho Iwai Corp. "The dollar's inability to rise lies outside of Japan," he said.

U.S. hedge fund operators are thought to be among those willing to sell dollars at around 108.50 and above, which would cap a dollar rally at 109 yen, although they are in no rush to sell dollars, Tokyo dealers said.
The dollar stood at around 108.30 yen at late Friday afternoon trade in Tokyo.

Persistent dollar selling by U.S. funds, including talk of sales by an influential financier, continued even after the release of the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) August quarterly survey on Wednesday that showed unexpectedly poor business sentiment in Japan.
"Their sales might be tied to uncertainty over the dollar's direction. They may want to cash in their profits in their dollar long positions built since last year," said Iida.
He said if the current issue over tax breaks in the U.S. presidential race heats up, that may push up U.S. interest rates and hurt stocks and the dollar.
Mitsuru Saito, senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd said: "U.S. fund sales may be based on expectations that the U.S. will raise interest rates in September at the earliest."

A rise in U.S. interest rates would increase demand for the dollar, but it would also in the short term push up the U.S. bond yield and hurt the stock market, cutting demand for dollars, dealers said.

The U.S. Commerce Department on Thursday revised up U.S. second quarter GDP growth to 4.8 percent against 4.2 percent previously. This fanned views in the money and bond markets that fast growth would lead to a rise in U.S. rates, although currency markets have not yet factored this in, dealers said.

"I think the Fed will raise its key interest rates by 25 basis points in September if economic indicators give further evidence of an expansion and fan inflationary fears," said a senior money trader at a European bank. "The U.S. presidential election would not be an absolute obstacle to rate hikes," he added.

Hiroyuki Murase, assistant vice president at Bank of America, said U.S. funds might try to square their dollar/yen positions and move their funds to marks to prepare for possible turmoil in European currencies over a plan for a single currency by 1999.

Many European nations will start budget talks for 1997 in September and there are doubts whether some nations such as France can meet strict criteria for monetary union, with operators more willing to buy the mark and the Swiss franc as safe haven currencies in Europe than dollars.
The selling of dollars against the yen has also stemmed from Japanese exporters which hope to cash in overseas profits ahead of their half-year book closings at the end of September.
Dealers said dollar sales related to maturing options positions with strike prices at around 108.50-109.00 yen have also limited the dollar's advance.

Tokyo dealers said despite heavy selling pressure, the greenback was not likely to fall below 105 yen because the U.S. and Japanese monetary authorities would act to halt its slide through dollar buying intervention.
